title: Temperature in space
summary: Why scientists use kelvin, how cold deep space is, and why the hottest planet is not the closest one.

badge.name: Thermometer
badge.text: You can read space temperatures in kelvin and explain why Venus beats Mercury.

steps.heading: A scale that starts at the bottom
body: Scientists measure temperature in kelvin (K). A step of one kelvin is the same size as one degree Celsius, but the scale starts at absolute zero, so there are no negative numbers.
Absolute zero is 0 K, which is -273.15 °C or -459.67 °F.

facts.text: A change of one kelvin is the same as a change of one degree Celsius.

checks.quote: A change of one kelvin is the same amount of temperature change as one degree Celsius

steps.heading: How cold is deep space?
body: Far from any star, the only warmth is a faint glow left over from the early universe, called the cosmic microwave background. It has a temperature of about 2.7 K, barely above absolute zero.
So space has no single temperature: it depends on where you are.

facts.text: The cosmic microwave background is about 2.7 K, measured by NASA's WMAP mission.

source.name: NASA WMAP: Tests of Big Bang, the CMB

steps.heading: Closer is not always hotter
body: The Sun is about 5,772 K at its visible surface and about 15.7 million K at its core.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, but Venus is hotter: Venus averages 737 K and Mercury 440 K. Venus's thick air is mostly carbon dioxide, which traps heat.

questions.prompt: About how cold is the cosmic microwave background, in kelvin?
questions.explanation: WMAP measured about 2.725 K, barely above absolute zero.

questions.prompt: Which planet has the higher average temperature?

choices.explanation: Mercury is closer to the Sun, but it is cooler on average.
Its carbon dioxide air traps heat.

questions.prompt: What is 0 K in degrees Celsius?

choices.explanation: 0 °C is where water freezes, far above absolute zero.
Colder than that is still possible.
